Pattern 11 of 24

Depth-First Search (DFS) on Graphs

Go as deep as you can down one path. When you hit a dead end, back up to the last fork and try the next road. A visited set makes sure you never walk in circles.

1. What is this pattern for?

Exploring a cave with a ball of string. At every fork you take the first unexplored tunnel and keep going. When you reach a dead end, you follow the string back to the last fork and try the next tunnel. You chalk an X on every chamber you've seen, so you never explore it twice. The string is the stack, and the chalk marks are the visited set.

A graph is a set of nodes (cities, courses, people, cells) joined by edges (roads, prerequisites, friendships). Unlike a tree, a graph can have cycles and nodes with many neighbours. It's usually given as an edge list [[a, b], ...], an adjacency matrix, or an adjacency list {node: [neighbours]}.

DFS answers reachability and structure questions:

  • Can I get from A to B? Which nodes can I reach at all?
  • How many separate groups (connected components) are there?
  • Is there a cycle? Can these tasks be ordered so every prerequisite comes first (topological sort)?
  • Enumerate all paths, clone a graph, or find bridges (edges whose removal disconnects the graph).

It does not find shortest paths. For that, see BFS.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Build an adjacency list. Turn the edge list into graph[u] = [v1, v2, ...]. For undirected edges, add both directions.
  2. Mark on entry. When you enter node u, add it to visited immediately. That alone prevents infinite loops on cycles.
  3. Recurse into every unvisited neighbour. for v in graph[u]: if v not in visited: dfs(v). Recursion remembers where to come back to.
  4. Backtrack automatically. When the loop ends, the function returns and you're back at the previous node. That's the "follow the string back" step. An explicit stack can do the same thing without recursion.
  5. Loop over all nodes for disconnected graphs. for u in all nodes: if u not visited: dfs(u). Each time this outer loop starts a new DFS, you've found a new component.
  6. Level up: three colours for directed graphs. White = unvisited, gray = on the current path, black = finished. Reaching a gray node means you've looped back onto your own path, so there's a cycle. Record nodes as they turn black, then reverse that list to get a topological order.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot DFS

Trigger words

  • "connected", "reachable", "path exists", "can you visit all"
  • "number of provinces / components / groups / islands"
  • "prerequisites", "dependencies", "order of tasks", "build order" → topological sort
  • "is there a cycle", "deadlock", "eventually safe"
  • "all paths from source to target", "clone / copy the graph"
  • "critical connection", "bridge", "articulation point"

Shape of the input

  • n plus an edge list, an adjacency list, or an n × n adjacency matrix.
  • Relations between entities: [course, prereq], [from, to], "a is friends with b".
  • The answer is yes/no, a count, or an ordering, not a minimum number of steps.
  • Brute-force smell: re-scanning the whole graph from every node (O(V·(V+E))), or exploring without a visited set and blowing up on cycles.
The one question to ask"Do I just need to explore everything reachable (or detect structure), rather than find the fewest steps?" If yes, use DFS. If it's fewest steps, use BFS.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use DFS when…Prefer something else when…
Reachability, counting components, flood-fill style explorationYou need the shortest path / fewest moves in an unweighted graph: use BFS
Cycle detection and topological sort (three colours)You'd like topological order level by level, or the "fewest semesters": use Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees), see BFS
Enumerating all paths in a DAG, cloning a graphYou enumerate choices (subsets, permutations) with undo: use Backtracking (DFS on a decision tree)
The structure is a general graph with cyclesIt's a rooted binary tree with no cycles: plain Tree Traversal, no visited set needed
The graph is a grid of cellsSame idea, but read Matrix Traversal for the 4-direction neighbour tricks
Results of sub-explorations repeatAdd memoization: Dynamic Programming on a DAG (e.g. longest increasing path)

Cost: O(V + E) time (each node entered once, each edge looked at once or twice), O(V) space for visited plus up to O(V) recursion/stack depth. With an adjacency matrix it's O(V²).

5. The Python templates (memorize these)

Five small building blocks. Every DFS problem below is one of these, slightly changed. Each block is followed by a plain-English walk-through.

0) Turn an edge list into an adjacency list

# 0) Edge list -> adjacency list
# graph[node] will be the list of nodes you can step to from node.
def build_graph(n, edges, directed=False):
    graph = {}
    # Give every node 0..n-1 an empty list first,
    # so graph[node] works even for a node with no edges.
    for node in range(n):
        graph[node] = []
    for edge in edges:
        from_node = edge[0]
        to_node = edge[1]
        graph[from_node].append(to_node)      # edge from_node -> to_node
        if not directed:
            graph[to_node].append(from_node)  # undirected: also add the way back
    return graph

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. We make an empty dict graph. It will map each node to the list of its neighbours.
  2. The first loop gives every node 0..n-1 an empty list. Now graph[node] never fails, even for a node with no edges.
  3. The second loop reads each edge [from_node, to_node] (one assignment per value, no unpacking) and appends to_node to from_node's list.
  4. If the graph is undirected (directed=False), the edge works both ways, so we also append from_node to to_node's list.

Dry run on build_graph(3, [[0, 1], [1, 2]]):

Edgegraph after it
(start){0: [], 1: [], 2: []}
[0, 1]{0: [1], 1: [0], 2: []}
[1, 2]{0: [1], 1: [0, 2], 2: [1]}

A) Recursive DFS + visited set

# A) Recursive DFS + visited set
# visited = set of nodes already entered, order = list that records the visit order.
def dfs(node, graph, visited, order):
    visited.add(node)                  # mark on ENTRY, before looking at neighbours
    order.append(node)                 # "do the work" for this node (here: remember it)
    for neighbour in graph[node]:
        if neighbour not in visited:   # only walk into tunnels we have not chalked yet
            dfs(neighbour, graph, visited, order)
    # when the loop ends, the function returns = we back up to the previous node

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. visited.add(node) chalks the node the moment we enter it. Doing this first is what stops infinite loops on cycles.
  2. order.append(node) is the "do the work" spot. Here we just record the visit order; in a real problem you might count, copy or check something.
  3. The for loop looks at every neighbour. If it isn't chalked yet, we call dfs on it: we dive deeper right away.
  4. When the loop finishes, the function returns. Python then continues the loop of the node that called us: that is the "back up the string" step, done for free by recursion.

Dry run on the graph {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 3], 2: [0, 4], 3: [1, 4], 4: [2, 3, 5], 5: [4]} from node 0:

CallWhat happensorder so far
dfs(0)mark 0, first neighbour 1 is new[0]
dfs(1)mark 1, neighbour 0 seen, 3 is new[0, 1]
dfs(3)mark 3, neighbour 1 seen, 4 is new[0, 1, 3]
dfs(4)mark 4, neighbour 2 is new[0, 1, 3, 4]
dfs(2)mark 2, neighbours 0 and 4 seen, return to 4[0, 1, 3, 4, 2]
dfs(5)back in 4: 3 seen, 5 is new; mark 5, then everything returns[0, 1, 3, 4, 2, 5]

B) Iterative DFS with an explicit stack

# B) Iterative DFS with an explicit stack (no recursion limit)
def dfs_iter(start, graph):
    visited = set()
    order = []
    stack = [start]                    # a plain list used as a stack
    while len(stack) > 0:
        node = stack.pop()             # pop() removes and returns the LAST item (newest)
        if node in visited:            # a node may be pushed twice: skip repeats
            continue
        visited.add(node)
        order.append(node)             # "do the work" for this node
        # Push neighbours from LAST to FIRST, so the FIRST neighbour
        # ends up on top of the stack and is popped next (same order as recursion).
        neighbours = graph[node]
        i = len(neighbours) - 1
        while i >= 0:
            neighbour = neighbours[i]
            if neighbour not in visited:
                stack.append(neighbour)
            i = i - 1
    return order

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Instead of recursion we keep our own stack (a list). append puts an item on top, pop() takes the top item off.
  2. Each round pops one node. A node can be pushed twice (by two different neighbours) before it is visited, so if it is already in visited we continue (skip it).
  3. Otherwise we mark it and record it.
  4. We push the neighbours from the last one to the first one with a while loop counting i down. The first neighbour is pushed last, so it sits on top and gets popped next. That gives the same order as the recursive version.
  5. When the stack is empty, every reachable node has been visited.

Dry run on the same graph from node 0 (the top of the stack is on the right):

C) Count connected components

# C) Count connected components (uses dfs from block A)
def count_components(n, graph):
    visited = set()
    components = 0
    for node in range(n):
        if node not in visited:        # nobody reached this node yet...
            components = components + 1  # ...so it starts a NEW component
            order = []                 # dfs wants an order list; we do not need it here
            dfs(node, graph, visited, order)  # chalk every node in this component
    return components

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. We try every node as a possible starting point.
  2. If the node is not in visited, no earlier DFS reached it, so it belongs to a component we haven't seen: add 1.
  3. Then we run dfs (block A) from it. That chalks the whole component, so none of its nodes will start a new count later.
  4. At the end, components is the number of fresh starts, which is the number of components.

Dry run on n = 5, edges [[0, 1], [1, 2], [3, 4]]:

nodealready visited?componentsvisited after

2yes1{0, 1, 2}
3no: new component, dfs chalks 3, 42{0, 1, 2, 3, 4}

D) Cycle detection + topological sort (3 colours)

# D) Cycle detection + topological sort (directed graph, 3 colours)
WHITE = 0   # never visited
GRAY = 1    # on the current path (we are still inside it)
BLACK = 2   # finished: everything below it has been explored


# Helper for topo_sort. Returns False if a cycle is found below node.
def visit(node, graph, color, post):
    color[node] = GRAY                 # node is now on the current path
    for neighbour in graph[node]:
        if color[neighbour] == GRAY:   # back edge to our own path -> cycle!
            return False
        if color[neighbour] == WHITE:
            found_no_cycle = visit(neighbour, graph, color, post)
            if not found_no_cycle:
                return False           # a cycle was found deeper down: pass it up
    color[node] = BLACK                # all neighbours finished -> node is finished
    post.append(node)                  # record the node in FINISH order
    return True


def topo_sort(n, graph):
    color = [WHITE] * n                # one colour per node, all start WHITE
    post = []                          # nodes in the order they finished
    for node in range(n):
        if color[node] == WHITE:
            ok = visit(node, graph, color, post)
            if not ok:
                return None            # cycle: no valid order exists
    # Reverse the finish order with a while loop -> topological order.
    order = []
    i = len(post) - 1
    while i >= 0:
        order.append(post[i])
        i = i - 1
    return order

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Three named numbers: WHITE (never seen), GRAY (on the path we are walking right now), BLACK (finished).
  2. visit is a separate top-level helper (no nested functions). It paints the node GRAY, then looks at each neighbour.
  3. A GRAY neighbour is on our own current path, so we have walked in a circle: return False (cycle).
  4. A WHITE neighbour is unexplored: visit it. If that deeper call found a cycle, pass the False straight up.
  5. A BLACK neighbour is already finished and safe, so we ignore it.
  6. After all neighbours, paint the node BLACK and append it to post. A node is appended only after everything it points to, so post lists "later" nodes first.
  7. topo_sort calls visit from every WHITE node (to cover disconnected parts). If any call reports a cycle, there is no order: return None.
  8. Finally it copies post backwards with a while loop. Reversed finish order = topological order.

Dry run on directed edges 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, 2→3:

Stepcolor (nodes 0..3)post
visit 0[1, 0, 0, 0][]
visit 1[1, 1, 0, 0][]
visit 3 (no neighbours), 3 finishes[1, 1, 0, 2][3]
1 finishes[1, 2, 0, 2][3, 1]
visit 2 (3 is BLACK: skip), 2 finishes[1, 2, 2, 2][3, 1, 2]
0 finishes[2, 2, 2, 2][3, 1, 2, 0]
reverse post[0, 2, 1, 3]

(1 = GRAY, 2 = BLACK.) Every edge goes left to right in [0, 2, 1, 3], so it is a valid order.

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Chalk, then dive"Chalk the chamber (mark visited) before diving into its tunnels. Dive deep, and back up only when you're stuck. For directed graphs, add traffic lights: white = never seen, gray = I'm still inside it, black = done. Hitting gray = you've driven in a circle.
How this hook works: what “Chalk, then dive” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Chalk”
Mark the node visited (visited.add(node)) the moment you enter it.
“then dive”
Go into the first neighbour you haven't chalked, and keep going deeper. Back up (return) only when every tunnel from here is chalked.
“traffic lights”
For directed graphs, use three colours instead of one chalk mark: white = never seen, gray = still on the current path, black = finished. Reaching a gray node means you drove in a circle.

Why this picture fits the pattern: DFS problems (connected components, islands, paths, cycles) are about exploring everything reachable. Chalk stops you exploring a room twice, and diving explains why recursion, or a stack, is the natural tool.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
A chambera node
Its tunnelsgraph[node]
Chalk markvisited.add(node) on entry
Divedfs(neighbour, …) for unvisited neighbours
Follow the string backthe function returns (the call stack)
Gray / blackstate[node] = 1 while inside, 2 when done

Watch it on numbers

Undirected edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3. Start at 0.

  1. Chalk 0 and dive into 1. Chalk 1. Its tunnel to 0 is chalked, so skip it. Dive into 3.
  2. Chalk 3. Its only tunnel (to 1) is chalked, so this is a dead end. Back up to 1, which has nothing left, then back up to 0.
  3. 0's next tunnel leads to 2. Chalk 2. Its tunnel to 0 is chalked, so back up.
  4. Visit order 0, 1, 3, 2. Without the chalk, 0 → 1 → 0 → 1 … would loop forever.

The trap it saves you from

Marking a node only when you leave it, or not at all: cycles then recurse forever. In Python, very deep recursion (more than about 1000 levels) also crashes, so switch to an explicit stack.

It still works when…

Counting components: "new start, new group". Every time the outer loop finds an unchalked node, that's a new component. Course Schedule: hitting a gray node means a cycle. Topological order is the finish order, reversed.

Picture

A person walking a maze with one hand always on the wall, unrolling string behind them. The string's length is the recursion depth.

Chant

"Mark, loop, recurse, return. New start, new group. Gray means loop."

Topo trick

"Finish last, list first." A node finishes only after everything it points to has finished, so reversing the finish order puts prerequisites first.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

New to this pattern? Start with theseSolve 1971. Find if Path Exists in Graph, then 547. Number of Provinces, then 133. Clone Graph. They are marked Start here below. Read the explanation, press Play on the step-through, then close the page and solve it yourself on LeetCode.
Medium 547. Number of Provinces Start here Google Meta Amazon GraphMatrix

Problem: isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly connected. A province is a group of cities connected directly or indirectly. Count the provinces.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: isConnected = [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]]
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: isConnected = [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]]
Output: 3

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 · n == isConnected.length · n == isConnected[i].length · isConnected[i][j] is 1 or 0. · isConnected[i][i] == 1 · isConnected[i][j] == isConnected[j][i]

Hint 1

Cities connected directly or indirectly form one province: a connected component.

Hint 2

For every unvisited city, run a DFS that marks its whole component; count how many DFS runs you start.

From brute force to the pattern: Repeatedly merging groups of cities by scanning the matrix is slow and fiddly. One DFS (or union-find) per unvisited city visits each city once and reads its matrix row: O(n²), which is the size of the input.

Spot it: "groups connected directly or indirectly" = connected components. The input is an adjacency matrix.

Key insight: Loop over cities. Each time you find an unvisited one, that's a new province: DFS from it to chalk-mark every city in that province.

Approach:

  1. Keep visited, a boolean per city.
  2. Loop over every city u. If it's unvisited, that's a new province: add 1.
  3. Run DFS from u: mark it, then recurse into every v with isConnected[u][v] == 1 that isn't visited yet.
  4. When the loop ends, the counter is the number of provinces.
class Solution:
    def findCircleNum(self, isConnected: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        city_count = len(isConnected)
        # Save the input on self so the dfs method can read it.
        self.isConnected = isConnected
        self.visited = [False] * city_count  # one flag per city, all start False
        provinces = 0
        for city in range(city_count):
            if not self.visited[city]:
                provinces = provinces + 1  # fresh start = a new province
                self.dfs(city)             # chalk every city in this province
        return provinces

    # Mark city, then dive into every connected city we have not visited yet.
    def dfs(self, city: int) -> None:
        self.visited[city] = True
        row = self.isConnected[city]   # row[other] == 1 means city and other are connected
        for other in range(len(row)):
            if row[other] == 1 and not self.visited[other]:
                self.dfs(other)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. findCircleNum stores the matrix and a visited list on self, so the separate dfs method can use them.
  2. It loops over every city. An unvisited city means a new province: add 1 to provinces.
  3. It then calls self.dfs(city), which marks every city in that province.
  4. dfs marks the city, takes its matrix row, and for every other city with row[other] == 1 that isn't visited, dives into it.
  5. When the outer loop ends, provinces holds the answer.

Dry run on isConnected = [[1,1,0],[1,1,0],[0,0,1]]:

Outer cityVisited before?dfs callsvisited afterprovinces
0nodfs(0) → dfs(1) (row 0 has a 1 at column 1)[True, True, False]1
1yesnone[True, True, False]1
2nodfs(2) (only connected to itself)[True, True, True]2

Edge cases to test:

  • No connections → n provinces.
  • Everyone connected → 1.
  • Indirect connections (A–B, B–C) form one province.

Complexity: O(n²) time (matrix input), O(n) space. Union-Find is an equally good alternative.

Medium 133. Clone Graph Start here Google Meta Amazon GraphHash Map

Problem: Given a reference to one node of a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy. Every node has val and a list of neighbors.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: adjList = [[2,4],[1,3],[2,4],[1,3]]
Output: [[2,4],[1,3],[2,4],[1,3]]
Explanation: There are 4 nodes in the graph. 1st node (val = 1)'s neighbors are 2nd node (val = 2) and 4th node (val = 4). 2nd node (val = 2)'s neighbors are 1st node (val = 1) and 3rd node (val = 3). 3rd node (val = 3)'s neighbors are 2nd node (val = 2) and 4th node (val = 4). 4th node (val = 4)'s neighbors are 1st node (val = 1) and 3rd node (val = 3).
Example 2
Input: adjList = [[]]
Output: [[]]
Explanation: Note that the input contains one empty list. The graph consists of only one node with val = 1 and it does not have any neighbors.

Constraints: The number of nodes in the graph is in the range [0, 100]. · 1 ≤ Node.val ≤ 100 · Node.val is unique for each node. · There are no repeated edges and no self-loops in the graph. · The Graph is connected and all nodes can be visited starting from the given node.

Hint 1

You must create a new node for every node and copy the edges, but the graph can have cycles.

Hint 2

Use a dictionary old node → copy: create a copy when you first see a node, and reuse it if you meet the node again.

From brute force to the pattern: Copying recursively without remembering what's already copied loops forever on cycles (or duplicates nodes). The old → new map acts as both the visited set and the lookup table: O(V + E).

Spot it: "copy every node reachable from here", and the graph has cycles. That's DFS with a visited map.

Key insight: Use a dict original → clone as the visited set. Register the clone before recursing into neighbours. Otherwise a cycle (A ↔ B) would try to clone A again forever.

Approach:

  1. Keep a dict copies mapping each original node to its clone. It doubles as the visited set.
  2. dfs(u): if u is already in copies, return its clone.
  3. Otherwise create the clone and store it in the dict before recursing.
  4. Fill the clone's neighbours with dfs(v) for each original neighbour, then return the clone.
class Solution:
    def cloneGraph(self, node: Optional['Node']) -> Optional['Node']:
        if node is None:               # empty graph -> nothing to copy
            return None
        self.copies = {}               # original node -> its clone (also our "visited" set)
        return self.clone(node)

    # Return the clone of original, creating it (and its neighbours) if needed.
    def clone(self, original: 'Node') -> 'Node':
        if original in self.copies:    # already cloned: reuse it (this stops cycles)
            return self.copies[original]
        copy = Node(original.val)
        self.copies[original] = copy   # register BEFORE recursing, so A <-> B ends
        for neighbour in original.neighbors:
            neighbour_copy = self.clone(neighbour)
            copy.neighbors.append(neighbour_copy)
        return copy

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If the input is None, there is nothing to copy.
  2. Otherwise we create the dict self.copies (original → clone) and start cloning from the given node.
  3. clone(original) first checks the dict. If this node was already cloned, it returns that clone. This is what stops the cycle A → B → A from going forever.
  4. Otherwise it makes a new Node with the same value and stores it in the dict before touching neighbours.
  5. Then for each original neighbour it gets (or makes) the neighbour's clone and appends it to the new node's neighbors list.

Dry run on adjList = [[2,4],[1,3],[2,4],[1,3]] (a square 1-2-3-4-1):

CallAlready in copies?copies (by value) after
clone(1)no: make 1{1}
clone(2) (1's first neighbour)no: make 2{1, 2}
clone(1) (2's first neighbour)yes: reuse{1, 2}
clone(3) (2's second neighbour)no: make 3{1, 2, 3}
clone(2) (3's first)yes: reuse{1, 2, 3}
clone(4) (3's second)no: make 4{1, 2, 3, 4}
clone(1), clone(3) (4's neighbours)yes, yes{1, 2, 3, 4}
clone(4) (1's second neighbour)yes: reuse{1, 2, 3, 4}

Edge cases to test:

  • An empty graph (None) → None.
  • A single node with no neighbours.
  • Cycles in the graph.

Complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V) space.

Medium 207. Course Schedule Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft Apple Graph

Problem: There are numCourses courses. [a, b] means you must take b before a. Can you finish them all?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: numCourses = 2, prerequisites = [[1,0]]
Output: true
Explanation: There are a total of 2 courses to take. To take course 1 you should have finished course 0. So it is possible.
Example 2
Input: numCourses = 2, prerequisites = [[1,0],[0,1]]
Output: false
Explanation: There are a total of 2 courses to take. To take course 1 you should have finished course 0, and to take course 0 you should also have finished course 1. So it is impossible.

Constraints: 1 ≤ numCourses ≤ 2000 · 0 ≤ prerequisites.length ≤ 5000 · prerequisites[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ai, bi < numCourses · All the pairs prerequisites[i] are unique.

Hint 1

Courses and prerequisites form a directed graph. When is finishing everything impossible?

Hint 2

It's impossible exactly when the graph has a cycle. Detect it with DFS colours (white/gray/black) or with Kahn's algorithm.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying course orders is factorial. Cycle detection with a three-colour DFS (a gray node met again means a cycle) or Kahn's topological sort runs in O(V + E).

Spot it: "prerequisites" = a directed graph. You can finish everything if and only if there's no cycle.

Key insight: Three-colour DFS. A gray node is on the current path. If you reach a gray node again, you've found a loop of courses that all wait on each other.

Approach:

  1. Build the graph with edges pre → course.
  2. Colour every node WHITE (0).
  3. has_cycle(u): paint u GRAY. For each neighbour, a GRAY one means a cycle; a WHITE one means recurse.
  4. After all neighbours are done, paint u BLACK and return False (no cycle through u).
  5. Run it from every WHITE node. The answer is True only if no call ever found a cycle.
class Solution:
    WHITE = 0   # never visited
    GRAY = 1    # on the current path
    BLACK = 2   # fully explored, known safe

    def canFinish(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> bool:
        # graph[pre] = list of courses that need pre first (edge pre -> course)
        self.graph = {}
        for course in range(numCourses):
            self.graph[course] = []
        for pair in prerequisites:
            course = pair[0]
            pre = pair[1]
            self.graph[pre].append(course)
        self.color = [self.WHITE] * numCourses  # every course starts WHITE
        for course in range(numCourses):
            if self.color[course] == self.WHITE:
                if self.has_cycle(course):
                    return False       # a loop of courses waiting on each other
        return True

    # Returns True if a cycle can be reached from course.
    def has_cycle(self, course: int) -> bool:
        self.color[course] = self.GRAY  # course is on the current path
        for next_course in self.graph[course]:
            if self.color[next_course] == self.GRAY:  # back edge -> cycle
                return True
            if self.color[next_course] == self.WHITE:
                if self.has_cycle(next_course):
                    return True
        self.color[course] = self.BLACK  # finished without finding a cycle
        return False

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Three class-level names WHITE, GRAY, BLACK make the colours readable (self.GRAY instead of a bare 1).
  2. We build self.graph: every course gets an empty list, then each pair [course, pre] adds the edge pre → course.
  3. Every course starts WHITE. We call has_cycle on each course that is still WHITE. If any call finds a cycle, the answer is False.
  4. has_cycle paints the course GRAY (it is on our current path), then checks each course that depends on it.
  5. A GRAY next course means we came back to our own path: cycle, return True. A WHITE one is explored recursively.
  6. If all next courses are fine, the course is painted BLACK (safe) and we return False.

Dry run on example 2, numCourses = 2, prerequisites = [[1,0],[0,1]] (graph {0: [1], 1: [0]}):

Stepcolor [course 0, course 1]Result
outer loop: course 0 is WHITE, call has_cycle(0)[GRAY, WHITE]
0's next course is 1 (WHITE): call has_cycle(1)[GRAY, GRAY]
1's next course is 0, which is GRAY[GRAY, GRAY]cycle → True
back in has_cycle(0): pass True up[GRAY, GRAY]canFinish returns False

With example 1 ([[1,0]]) the same steps paint 1 then 0 BLACK and the answer is True.

Edge cases to test:

  • No prerequisites → True.
  • A self-loop like [0, 0] → False.
  • Several disconnected groups of courses.

Complexity: O(V + E) time and space.

Medium 210. Course Schedule II Google Amazon Microsoft Apple Netflix Graph

Problem: Same input as 207, but return an order in which to take all courses, or [] if that's impossible.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: numCourses = 2, prerequisites = [[1,0]]
Output: [0,1]
Explanation: There are a total of 2 courses to take. To take course 1 you should have finished course 0. So the correct course order is [0,1].
Example 2
Input: numCourses = 4, prerequisites = [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]]
Output: [0,2,1,3]
Explanation: There are a total of 4 courses to take. To take course 3 you should have finished both courses 1 and 2. Both courses 1 and 2 should be taken after you finished course 0. So one correct course order is [0,1,2,3]. Another correct ordering is [0,2,1,3].

Constraints: 1 ≤ numCourses ≤ 2000 · 0 ≤ prerequisites.length ≤ numCourses * (numCourses - 1) · prerequisites[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ai, bi < numCourses · ai != bi · All the pairs [ai, bi] are distinct.

Hint 1

A valid order is a topological order of the prerequisite graph.

Hint 2

Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly take a course with no remaining prerequisites; or append courses in DFS post-order and reverse.

From brute force to the pattern: Generating orders and checking them is factorial. A topological sort produces a valid order (or detects a cycle) in O(V + E).

Spot it: "return an ordering that respects dependencies" = topological sort.

Key insight: In DFS, a course turns black only after every course that depends on it has turned black. So the finish order lists dependents first. Reverse it to put prerequisites first.

Approach:

  1. Build the graph pre → course and colour every node WHITE.
  2. visit(u): paint it GRAY and explore its neighbours. If you hit a GRAY node, report a cycle.
  3. When u finishes, paint it BLACK and append it to post.
  4. Visit every WHITE node. If any cycle was found, return [].
  5. Return post reversed. Every course now comes after all of its prerequisites.
class Solution:
    WHITE = 0   # never visited
    GRAY = 1    # on the current path
    BLACK = 2   # finished

    def findOrder(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        # graph[pre] = list of courses that need pre first (edge pre -> course)
        self.graph = {}
        for course in range(numCourses):
            self.graph[course] = []
        for pair in prerequisites:
            course = pair[0]
            pre = pair[1]
            self.graph[pre].append(course)
        self.color = [self.WHITE] * numCourses
        self.post = []                 # courses in the order they FINISH
        for course in range(numCourses):
            if self.color[course] == self.WHITE:
                if not self.visit(course):
                    return []          # cycle -> impossible
        # Reverse the finish order (prerequisites end up first).
        order = []
        i = len(self.post) - 1
        while i >= 0:
            order.append(self.post[i])
            i = i - 1
        return order

    # Returns False if a cycle is found below course.
    def visit(self, course: int) -> bool:
        self.color[course] = self.GRAY
        for next_course in self.graph[course]:
            if self.color[next_course] == self.GRAY:
                return False           # cycle
            if self.color[next_course] == self.WHITE:
                if not self.visit(next_course):
                    return False
        self.color[course] = self.BLACK
        self.post.append(course)       # finished: everything after it is placed
        return True

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Same graph as 207: every course gets a list, and each pair [course, pre] adds pre → course.
  2. self.color starts all WHITE and self.post (finish order) starts empty.
  3. We call visit on every WHITE course. If it returns False a cycle exists, so we return [].
  4. visit paints the course GRAY, explores each next course (GRAY = cycle, WHITE = recurse), then paints it BLACK and appends it to post.
  5. At the end we copy post backwards with a while loop. Courses that finish last (the ones with no prerequisites) come out first.

Dry run on numCourses = 4, prerequisites = [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]] (graph {0: [1, 2], 1: [3], 2: [3], 3: []}):

Stepcolor (0..3)post
visit 0[G, W, W, W][]
visit 1[G, G, W, W][]
visit 3, no next courses: 3 finishes[G, G, W, B][3]
1 finishes[G, B, W, B][3, 1]
visit 2 (3 is BLACK: skip), 2 finishes[G, B, B, B][3, 1, 2]
0 finishes[B, B, B, B][3, 1, 2, 0]
reverse post → answer[0, 2, 1, 3]

Edge cases to test:

  • A cycle → [].
  • No prerequisites → any order of all courses.
  • Isolated courses must still appear in the answer.

Complexity: O(V + E) time and space.

Hard 1192. Critical Connections in a Network Google Amazon Graph

Problem: n servers and undirected connections. A connection is critical if removing it disconnects some servers. Return all critical connections (these are called bridges).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 4, connections = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[1,3]]
Output: [[1,3]]
Explanation: [[3,1]] is also accepted.
Example 2
Input: n = 2, connections = [[0,1]]
Output: [[0,1]]

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · n - 1 ≤ connections.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ ai, bi ≤ n - 1 · ai != bi · There are no repeated connections.

Hint 1

An edge is critical if removing it disconnects the graph: it lies on no cycle.

Hint 2

Tarjan's algorithm: DFS discovery times plus the lowest discovery time reachable from each subtree. Edge (u, v) is a bridge if low[v] > disc[u].

From brute force to the pattern: Removing each edge and checking connectivity is O(E · (V + E)). Tarjan's bridge-finding DFS identifies every critical edge in one pass: O(V + E).

Spot it: "removing an edge disconnects the graph" = bridges, which Tarjan's DFS finds in one pass.

Key insight: Stamp each node with its discovery time disc[u]. Let low[u] be the earliest discovery time reachable from u's DFS subtree using one back edge. If a child v can't reach anything discovered at or before u (low[v] > disc[u]), the only way out of v's subtree is the edge u–v, so it's a bridge. An edge on a cycle is never a bridge.

Approach:

  1. Build an undirected adjacency list. disc[u] = -1 marks unvisited.
  2. DFS from node 0, giving each node a discovery time disc[u] and starting with low[u] = disc[u].
  3. For each neighbour v other than the parent: if unvisited, recurse, then set low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]).
  4. Right after recursing into v: if low[v] > disc[u], nothing in v's subtree can reach u or above without the edge u–v, so it's a bridge.
  5. If v was already visited (a back edge), set low[u] = min(low[u], disc[v]).
class Solution:
    def criticalConnections(self, n: int, connections: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        # Undirected adjacency list: add each connection in both directions.
        self.graph = {}
        for server in range(n):
            self.graph[server] = []
        for connection in connections:
            server_a = connection[0]
            server_b = connection[1]
            self.graph[server_a].append(server_b)
            self.graph[server_b].append(server_a)
        self.disc = [-1] * n           # discovery time (-1 = not visited yet)
        self.low = [0] * n             # earliest disc reachable from the subtree
        self.bridges = []
        self.timer = 0                 # the next discovery time to hand out
        self.dfs(0, -1)                # the network is connected; 0 has no parent
        return self.bridges

    def dfs(self, node: int, parent: int) -> None:
        self.disc[node] = self.timer   # stamp the discovery time
        self.low[node] = self.timer    # at first, node can only reach itself
        self.timer = self.timer + 1
        for neighbour in self.graph[node]:
            if neighbour == parent:
                continue               # don't use the edge we came in on
            if self.disc[neighbour] == -1:  # tree edge: explore it
                self.dfs(neighbour, node)
                self.low[node] = min(self.low[node], self.low[neighbour])
                if self.low[neighbour] > self.disc[node]:
                    # neighbour's subtree can't climb above node -> bridge
                    self.bridges.append([node, neighbour])
            else:                      # back edge to an ancestor
                self.low[node] = min(self.low[node], self.disc[neighbour])

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. We build an undirected adjacency list on self.graph (each connection added both ways).
  2. self.disc holds each server's discovery time (-1 = not visited). self.low holds the earliest discovery time the server's subtree can reach. self.timer is the next time stamp.
  3. We start dfs(0, -1): server 0 with no parent.
  4. In dfs, we stamp disc and low with the timer and move the timer on.
  5. For each neighbour: skip the parent (that's the edge we came in on). An unvisited neighbour is a tree edge: recurse, then pull its low up into ours. If low[neighbour] > disc[node], the neighbour's subtree has no other way back, so the edge is a bridge.
  6. A visited neighbour that isn't the parent is a back edge: it lets us reach disc[neighbour], so low[node] may drop to that.

Dry run on n = 4, connections = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[1,3]] (graph {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 2, 3], 2: [1, 0], 3: [1]}):

Stepdisclowbridges
enter 0, 1, 2 (tree edges 0–1, 1–2)[0, 1, 2, -1][0, 1, 2, 0][]
at 2: neighbour 0 already visited (back edge) → low[2] = 0; leave 2[0, 1, 2, -1][0, 1, 0, 0][]
back at 1: low[1] = min(1, 0) = 0; is low[2]=0 > disc[1]=1? no[0, 1, 2, -1][0, 0, 0, 0][]
enter 3 (only neighbour is the parent); leave 3[0, 1, 2, 3][0, 0, 0, 3][]
back at 1: is low[3]=3 > disc[1]=1? yes → bridge[0, 1, 2, 3][0, 0, 0, 3][[1, 3]]
back at 0: low[1]=0 is not > 0; neighbour 2 already visited[0, 1, 2, 3][0, 0, 0, 3][[1, 3]]

(low[3] shows 0 before 3 is entered only because low starts as all zeros; it is overwritten when 3 is discovered.)

Edge cases to test:

  • A tree (every edge is critical).
  • One big cycle → [].
  • Ignore the edge back to your DFS parent when updating low.

Complexity: O(V + E) time and space. For n = 105 in Python, raise the recursion limit or convert to an iterative DFS.

8. Common mistakes

Marking visited too lateIf you mark a node visited only after exploring its neighbours, a cycle sends you round forever (or you push the same node many times). Mark on entry.
Using a plain visited set for directed cycle detectionIn a directed graph, reaching an already-visited node is not always a cycle (it may be a finished side branch). You need gray vs. black, i.e. "on the current path" vs. "finished".
Forgetting disconnected partsOne dfs(0) only explores node 0's component. Wrap it in for u in range(n).
Wrong edge directionFor [course, prereq], decide once whether the edge is prereq → course or the reverse, and keep it consistent. Otherwise your topological order comes out backwards.
Treating the parent as a cycle in undirected graphsIn an undirected graph every edge appears twice, so your parent always looks "visited". Skip the parent, or use the 3-colour method only for directed graphs.
Recursion depthPython's default limit is about 1000 frames. For large inputs call sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6) or switch to the explicit-stack template.

9. Self-check quiz

During 3-colour DFS on a directed graph, a cycle is proven when you reach…

Gray means "still on my current path". Reaching one means the path loops back on itself. Black nodes are finished and safe; white ones are just unexplored.

"Minimum number of moves for a knight to reach a square." DFS or BFS?

"Minimum moves" in an unweighted graph is a shortest-path question. BFS explores in rings of increasing distance, so the first time it reaches the target is optimal. DFS gives no such guarantee.

When counting connected components, the answer is…

Each new DFS from an unvisited node floods one whole component, so every fresh start is exactly one component.

A topological order from DFS is…

A node finishes after all of its descendants. Reversing the finish order puts every node before the nodes it points to.

Easy 1971. Find if Path Exists in Graph Start here Meta Amazon Microsoft GraphHash SetStack

Problem: Given n nodes and an undirected edge list, is there a path from source to destination?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0]], source = 0, destination = 2
Output: true
Explanation: There are two paths from vertex 0 to vertex 2: - 0 → 1 → 2 - 0 → 2
Example 2
Input: n = 6, edges = [[0,1],[0,2],[3,5],[5,4],[4,3]], source = 0, destination = 5
Output: false
Explanation: There is no path from vertex 0 to vertex 5.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 2 * 10⁵ · 0 ≤ edges.length ≤ 2 * 10⁵ · edges[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ui, vi ≤ n - 1 · ui != vi · 0 ≤ source, destination ≤ n - 1 · There are no duplicate edges. · There are no self edges.

Hint 1

Build an adjacency list from the edges.

Hint 2

DFS or BFS from source, marking visited nodes; check whether destination gets visited.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every path is exponential. A traversal visits each vertex and edge once: O(V + E). Union-find is another good option.

Spot it: "is there a path" is plain reachability. DFS from the source and see if you reach the destination.

Approach:

  1. Build an adjacency list (both directions).
  2. Push source onto a stack and mark it seen.
  3. Pop a node. If it's the destination, return True. Otherwise push its unseen neighbours, marking them as you push.
  4. If the stack empties first, return False.
class Solution:
    def validPath(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]], source: int, destination: int) -> bool:
        graph = {}
        for node in range(n):
            graph[node] = []
        for edge in edges:
            node_a = edge[0]
            node_b = edge[1]
            graph[node_a].append(node_b)
            graph[node_b].append(node_a)   # undirected: add both directions
        seen = set()
        seen.add(source)
        stack = [source]               # a plain list used as a stack
        while len(stack) > 0:
            node = stack.pop()         # pop() takes the newest item off the top
            if node == destination:
                return True
            for neighbour in graph[node]:
                if neighbour not in seen:
                    seen.add(neighbour)    # mark when pushed: never pushed twice
                    stack.append(neighbour)
        return False                   # stack empty: destination never reached

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Build the adjacency list: every node gets an empty list, then each edge is added in both directions.
  2. Put source in seen and on the stack.
  3. While the stack isn't empty, pop the top node. If it is the destination, we found a path: return True.
  4. Otherwise push every neighbour we haven't seen, marking it as seen at push time so it is never pushed twice.
  5. If the stack runs out, the destination is unreachable: return False.

Dry run on n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0]], source = 0, destination = 2 (graph {0: [1, 2], 1: [0, 2], 2: [1, 0]}):

PopIs it 2?Pushedstack afterseen after
(start)[0]{0}
0no1, 2[1, 2]{0, 1, 2}
2yes → return True[1]{0, 1, 2}

Edge cases to test:

  • source == destination → True.
  • No edges at all.
  • Disconnected components.

Complexity: O(V + E) time and space.

Medium 841. Keys and Rooms Google Meta Apple GraphHash SetStack

Problem: Room 0 is unlocked, and every other room is locked. rooms[i] lists the keys you find inside room i. Can you get into every room?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: rooms = [[1],[2],[3],[]]
Output: true
Explanation: We visit room 0 and pick up key 1. We then visit room 1 and pick up key 2. We then visit room 2 and pick up key 3. We then visit room 3. Since we were able to visit every room, we return true.
Example 2
Input: rooms = [[1,3],[3,0,1],[2],[0]]
Output: false
Explanation: We can not enter room number 2 since the only key that unlocks it is in that room.

Constraints: n == rooms.length · 2 ≤ n ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ rooms[i].length ≤ 1000 · 1 ≤ sum(rooms[i].length) ≤ 3000 · 0 ≤ rooms[i][j] < n · All the values of rooms[i] are unique.

Hint 1

Rooms are nodes and keys are edges. Can you reach every room from room 0?

Hint 2

DFS from room 0, collecting keys; at the end, compare the number of visited rooms with n.

From brute force to the pattern: Repeatedly scanning all rooms for ones you can now open is O(n²). A single DFS/BFS from room 0 over the key graph is O(rooms + keys).

Spot it: Rooms are nodes and keys are directed edges. "Can I visit all?" means: does a DFS from room 0 reach every node?

Approach:

  1. Start with seen = {0} and a stack [0].
  2. Pop a room, and for each key that opens an unseen room, mark that room and push it.
  3. At the end, compare the number of rooms seen with the total.
class Solution:
    def canVisitAllRooms(self, rooms: List[List[int]]) -> bool:
        seen = set()
        seen.add(0)                    # room 0 is unlocked
        stack = [0]                    # rooms we can enter but have not searched yet
        while len(stack) > 0:
            room = stack.pop()         # pop() takes the newest room off the top
            for key in rooms[room]:    # each key = an edge room -> key
                if key not in seen:
                    seen.add(key)
                    stack.append(key)
        return len(seen) == len(rooms)  # did we reach every room?

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Room 0 is open, so it starts in seen and on the stack.
  2. Pop a room and look at each key inside it.
  3. A key to a room we haven't seen: mark that room seen and push it so we search it later.
  4. When the stack is empty we have searched every room we can open. Compare how many we saw with the total.

Dry run on rooms = [[1],[2],[3],[]]:

Pop roomKeys insidestack afterseen after
0[1][1]{0, 1}
1[2][2]{0, 1, 2}
2[3][3]{0, 1, 2, 3}
3[][]{0, 1, 2, 3}

4 rooms seen out of 4, so the answer is True.

Edge cases to test:

  • Room 0 contains no keys.
  • Keys to rooms that are already open.
  • A key to room 0 itself.

Complexity: O(rooms + keys) time, O(rooms) space.

Medium 797. All Paths From Source to Target Amazon Netflix Graph

Problem: Given a DAG (directed graph with no cycles) as an adjacency list, return every path from node 0 to node n-1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: graph = [[1,2],[3],[3],[]]
Output: [[0,1,3],[0,2,3]]
Explanation: There are two paths: 0 -> 1 -> 3 and 0 -> 2 -> 3.
Example 2
Input: graph = [[4,3,1],[3,2,4],[3],[4],[]]
Output: [[0,4],[0,3,4],[0,1,3,4],[0,1,2,3,4],[0,1,4]]

Constraints: n == graph.length · 2 ≤ n ≤ 15 · 0 ≤ graph[i][j] < n · graph[i][j] != i (i.e., there will be no self-loops). · All the elements of graph[i] are unique. · The input graph is guaranteed to be a DAG.

Hint 1

The graph is a DAG, so paths can't loop.

Hint 2

Backtracking DFS: extend the path, recurse into each neighbour, record the path when you reach n − 1, then pop.

From brute force to the pattern: There's no shortcut: the output itself can be exponential in size. Backtracking enumerates each path exactly once without needing a visited set, because there are no cycles.

Spot it: "all paths" means explore every branch, which is DFS. The graph has no cycles, so no visited set is needed.

Approach:

  1. Keep the current path (it starts as [0]).
  2. dfs(u): if u is the target, save a copy of the path.
  3. Otherwise, for each neighbour v: append it, recurse, then pop it (undo, backtracking-style).
class Solution:
    def allPathsSourceTarget(self, graph: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        self.graph = graph
        self.target = len(graph) - 1
        self.result = []
        self.path = [0]                # the path we are walking right now
        self.dfs(0)
        return self.result

    def dfs(self, node: int) -> None:
        if node == self.target:
            path_copy = list(self.path)  # copy! self.path keeps changing afterwards
            self.result.append(path_copy)
            return
        for next_node in self.graph[node]:
            self.path.append(next_node)  # choose
            self.dfs(next_node)          # explore
            self.path.pop()              # un-choose (backtrack)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. allPathsSourceTarget saves the graph, the target n-1, an empty result and the current path = [0] on self, then calls dfs(0).
  2. In dfs, if we are at the target, we append a copy of the path (list(self.path)). Without the copy, later pop() calls would change the saved path too.
  3. Otherwise for each next node: append it to the path (choose), recurse (explore), then pop it off again (un-choose) so the path is ready for the next branch.
  4. No visited set: the graph is a DAG, so we can never loop.

Dry run on graph = [[1,2],[3],[3],[]] (target = 3):

Callpathresult
dfs(0)[0][]
dfs(1)[0, 1][]
dfs(3): target, save a copy[0, 1, 3][[0, 1, 3]]
pop 3, pop 1; dfs(2)[0, 2][[0, 1, 3]]
dfs(3): target, save a copy[0, 2, 3][[0, 1, 3], [0, 2, 3]]

Edge cases to test:

  • A direct edge from 0 to n − 1.
  • Several paths that share a prefix.
  • A node with no outgoing edges.

Complexity: O(2n · n) in the worst case, since there can be exponentially many paths. Extra space is O(n) on top of the output.

Medium 802. Find Eventual Safe States Amazon Microsoft Graph

Problem: In a directed graph, a node is safe if every path starting from it ends at a terminal node (one with no outgoing edges). Return all safe nodes in sorted order.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: graph = [[1,2],[2,3],[5],[0],[5],[],[]]
Output: [2,4,5,6]
Explanation: The given graph is shown above. Nodes 5 and 6 are terminal nodes as there are no outgoing edges from either of them. Every path starting at nodes 2, 4, 5, and 6 all lead to either node 5 or 6.
Example 2
Input: graph = [[1,2,3,4],[1,2],[3,4],[0,4],[]]
Output: [4]
Explanation: Only node 4 is a terminal node, and every path starting at node 4 leads to node 4.

Constraints: n == graph.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴ · 0 ≤ graph[i].length ≤ n · 0 ≤ graph[i][j] ≤ n - 1 · graph[i] is sorted in a strictly increasing order. · The graph may contain self-loops. · The number of edges in the graph will be in the range [1, 4 * 10⁴].

Hint 1

A node is safe if every path from it ends at a terminal node, i.e. it can't reach a cycle.

Hint 2

Three-colour DFS: a node is safe if its DFS finishes without meeting a gray node (or run a topological sort on the reversed graph).

From brute force to the pattern: Exploring all paths from every node is exponential. Colouring nodes once (unvisited / in progress / safe) gives each node's status in O(V + E).

Spot it: A node is unsafe exactly when it can reach a cycle. That's 3-colour DFS, and the final colours give the answer.

Approach:

  1. color[u]: 0 = unvisited, 1 = GRAY (on the path, or proven unsafe), 2 = BLACK (safe).
  2. safe(u): if it's already coloured, return color[u] == 2.
  3. Otherwise paint it GRAY and check every neighbour. If any neighbour is unsafe, return False and leave u GRAY, so it stays marked unsafe.
  4. If every neighbour is safe, paint u BLACK and return True.
  5. Return every u in 0..n-1 with safe(u) True.
class Solution:
    def eventualSafeNodes(self, graph: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        node_count = len(graph)
        self.graph = graph
        self.color = [0] * node_count  # 0 white, 1 gray/unsafe, 2 black/safe
        safe_nodes = []
        for node in range(node_count):  # 0..n-1 in order, so the answer is sorted
            if self.safe(node):
                safe_nodes.append(node)
        return safe_nodes

    def safe(self, node: int) -> bool:
        if self.color[node] != 0:      # already decided (or on the current path)
            return self.color[node] == 2  # gray here = on a cycle (or leads to one)
        self.color[node] = 1           # gray: on the current path
        for next_node in self.graph[node]:
            if not self.safe(next_node):
                return False           # node stays GRAY forever = unsafe
        self.color[node] = 2           # every path from node ends at a terminal node
        return True

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. self.color starts all 0 (white). We ask safe(node) for every node in order, and keep the safe ones. Going 0, 1, 2... means the answer comes out sorted.
  2. In safe, a node that already has a colour is answered at once: BLACK (2) means safe, GRAY (1) means it is on a cycle or leads to one.
  3. Otherwise we paint it GRAY and check every next node. If any of them is unsafe, we return False and leave this node GRAY on purpose: GRAY now also means "unsafe".
  4. If every next node is safe, the node is painted BLACK and we return True.

Edge cases to test:

  • Terminal nodes (no outgoing edges) are safe.
  • Self-loops are unsafe.
  • A node that can reach a cycle is unsafe even if some of its paths end.

Complexity: O(V + E) time and space.

Medium 399. Evaluate Division Google Amazon Microsoft GraphHash Map

Problem: You're given equations like a / b = 2.0. Answer queries like a / c. Return -1.0 if a query can't be determined.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: equations = [["a","b"],["b","c"]], values = [2.0,3.0], queries = [["a","c"],["b","a"],["a","e"],["a","a"],["x","x"]]
Output: [6.00000,0.50000,-1.00000,1.00000,-1.00000]
Explanation: Given: a / b = 2.0, b / c = 3.0 queries are: a / c = ?, b / a = ?, a / e = ?, a / a = ?, x / x = ? return: [6.0, 0.5, -1.0, 1.0, -1.0 ] note: x is undefined => -1.0
Example 2
Input: equations = [["a","b"],["b","c"],["bc","cd"]], values = [1.5,2.5,5.0], queries = [["a","c"],["c","b"],["bc","cd"],["cd","bc"]]
Output: [3.75000,0.40000,5.00000,0.20000]

Constraints: 1 ≤ equations.length ≤ 20 · equations[i].length == 2 · 1 ≤ Ai.length, Bi.length ≤ 5 · values.length == equations.length · 0.0 < values[i] ≤ 20.0 · 1 ≤ queries.length ≤ 20 · queries[i].length == 2 · 1 ≤ Cj.length, Dj.length ≤ 5 · Ai, Bi, Cj, Dj consist of lower case English letters and digits.

Hint 1

a / b = 2 is an edge a → b with weight 2 and b → a with weight ½.

Hint 2

A query x / y is the product of the weights along any path from x to y; find it with DFS.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying to solve the equations algebraically is complicated. Modelling the equations as a weighted graph and multiplying along a DFS path answers each query in O(V + E).

Spot it: Variables are nodes, and a/b = k is an edge a→b with weight k (plus b→a with weight 1/k). A query is "find any path and multiply the weights along it", which DFS can do.

Approach:

  1. Build a weighted graph: graph[a][b] = k and graph[b][a] = 1/k.
  2. For each query (x, y): if either variable is unknown, the answer is -1.
  3. Otherwise DFS from x with a fresh visited set. When you reach y, return 1.
  4. On the way back up, multiply by each edge's weight. If no neighbour leads to y, return -1.
class Solution:
    def calcEquation(self, equations: List[List[str]], values: List[float],
                     queries: List[List[str]]) -> List[float]:
        # graph[a][b] = the value of a / b
        self.graph = {}
        for i in range(len(equations)):
            top = equations[i][0]
            bottom = equations[i][1]
            value = values[i]
            if top not in self.graph:
                self.graph[top] = {}
            if bottom not in self.graph:
                self.graph[bottom] = {}
            self.graph[top][bottom] = value      # top / bottom = value
            self.graph[bottom][top] = 1 / value  # bottom / top = 1 / value
        answers = []
        for query in queries:
            start = query[0]
            target = query[1]
            if start in self.graph and target in self.graph:
                answers.append(self.dfs(start, target, set()))
            else:
                answers.append(-1.0)   # unknown variable
        return answers

    # Returns node / target by walking a path, or -1.0 if there is no path.
    def dfs(self, node: str, target: str, seen: set) -> float:
        if node == target:
            return 1.0                 # x / x = 1
        seen.add(node)
        for neighbour in self.graph[node]:
            if neighbour not in seen:
                rest = self.dfs(neighbour, target, seen)
                if rest != -1.0:
                    weight = self.graph[node][neighbour]  # node / neighbour
                    return weight * rest  # node/target = (node/neighbour) * (neighbour/target)
        return -1.0

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. We build self.graph as a dict of dicts. For top / bottom = value we store graph[top][bottom] = value and the reverse graph[bottom][top] = 1 / value. Each variable's inner dict is created the first time we see it.
  2. For each query [start, target]: if either variable never appeared in an equation, the answer is -1.0.
  3. Otherwise we call dfs(start, target, set()) with a fresh seen set.
  4. In dfs: reaching the target returns 1.0. Otherwise we mark the node seen and try each unseen neighbour. If a neighbour finds the target (rest != -1.0), we multiply by the edge weight on the way back: node/target = (node/neighbour) × (neighbour/target).
  5. If no neighbour leads to the target, return -1.0.

QueryDFS pathReturned values (inner to outer)Answer
a / ca → b → cc: 1.0, b: 3.0 × 1.0 = 3.0, a: 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.06.0
b / ab → aa: 1.0, b: 0.5 × 1.00.5
a / enone (e unknown)-1.0
a / aaa is the target: 1.01.0
x / xnone (x unknown)-1.0

Edge cases to test:

  • A variable that never appears → −1.0.
  • x / x for a known variable → 1.0.
  • Variables in different components → −1.0.

Complexity: O(Q · (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space.

Hard 332. Reconstruct Itinerary Google Apple Netflix GraphHash Map

Problem: Given airline tickets [from, to], use every ticket exactly once to build an itinerary starting at "JFK". If several work, return the lexicographically smallest one.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: tickets = [["MUC","LHR"],["JFK","MUC"],["SFO","SJC"],["LHR","SFO"]]
Output: ["JFK","MUC","LHR","SFO","SJC"]
Example 2
Input: tickets = [["JFK","SFO"],["JFK","ATL"],["SFO","ATL"],["ATL","JFK"],["ATL","SFO"]]
Output: ["JFK","ATL","JFK","SFO","ATL","SFO"]
Explanation: Another possible reconstruction is ["JFK","SFO","ATL","JFK","ATL","SFO"] but it is larger in lexical order.

Constraints: 1 ≤ tickets.length ≤ 300 · tickets[i].length == 2 · fromi.length == 3 · toi.length == 3 · fromi and toi consist of uppercase English letters. · fromi != toi

Hint 1

You must use every ticket exactly once: an Eulerian path starting at JFK.

Hint 2

Hierholzer's algorithm: always take the lexicographically smallest unused ticket; add an airport to the route when you get stuck, then reverse.

From brute force to the pattern: Backtracking over ticket orders can be exponential. Hierholzer's algorithm (with sorted destinations, consumed as you go) builds the itinerary in O(E log E).

Spot it: "use every edge exactly once" is an Euler path. Hierholzer's algorithm is a DFS that adds a node to the route when it gets stuck (postorder).

Approach:

  1. Build adjacency lists sorted in reverse order, so pop() always returns the smallest destination.
  2. visit(a): while a still has unused tickets, pop the smallest destination and visit it. Popping uses up the ticket.
  3. When a has no tickets left, append a to route (postorder).
  4. Dead ends get appended first, so reverse route at the end.
class Solution:
    def findItinerary(self, tickets: List[List[str]]) -> List[str]:
        # Sort tickets from LARGEST to smallest, so that when we append them,
        # the smallest destination ends up LAST in each list and pop() returns it.
        sorted_tickets = sorted(tickets, reverse=True)
        self.graph = {}
        for ticket in sorted_tickets:
            start = ticket[0]
            end = ticket[1]
            if start not in self.graph:
                self.graph[start] = []
            if end not in self.graph:
                self.graph[end] = []   # every airport gets a list, even with no tickets out
            self.graph[start].append(end)
        self.route = []
        self.visit("JFK")
        # Dead ends were added first, so reverse the route with a while loop.
        answer = []
        i = len(self.route) - 1
        while i >= 0:
            answer.append(self.route[i])
            i = i - 1
        return answer

    def visit(self, airport: str) -> None:
        while len(self.graph[airport]) > 0:   # tickets still unused from here
            next_airport = self.graph[airport].pop()  # pop() uses up the ticket
            self.visit(next_airport)
        self.route.append(airport)     # stuck -> add in POSTorder

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. We sort the tickets from largest to smallest. Appending in that order puts the smallest destination at the end of each list, where pop() takes from.
  2. We build self.graph: each airport gets a list (even airports with no tickets out), and each ticket appends its destination.
  3. visit(airport): while this airport still has unused tickets, pop the smallest destination (this uses the ticket up) and visit it.
  4. When an airport has no tickets left, we are stuck there, so we append it to self.route. This is post-order: the final stop is appended first.
  5. Finally we copy self.route backwards with a while loop to get the itinerary from JFK.

visit MUC, pop LHRLHR→SFO, SFO→SJC[]

visit SJC: stuck(none)["SJC"]

Edge cases to test:

  • A dead end reached early (that's why airports are added on the way back).
  • Duplicate tickets.
  • Lexicographic ties.

Complexity: O(E log E) time (sorting), O(E) space.

Hard 329. Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix Google Microsoft Matrix

Problem: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing path in a grid, moving up, down, left or right.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: matrix = [[9,9,4],[6,6,8],[2,1,1]]
Output: 4
Explanation: The longest increasing path is [1, 2, 6, 9].
Example 2
Input: matrix = [[3,4,5],[3,2,6],[2,2,1]]
Output: 4
Explanation: The longest increasing path is [3, 4, 5, 6]. Moving diagonally is not allowed.

Constraints: m == matrix.length · n == matrix[i].length · 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 200 · 0 ≤ matrix[i][j] ≤ 2³¹ - 1

Hint 1

From each cell, the longest increasing path depends only on the cells it can move to.

Hint 2

DFS with memoisation: best(cell) = 1 + max(best(neighbour)) over strictly larger neighbours.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS from every cell without memory recomputes the same paths over and over (exponential). The "strictly increasing" rule means there are no cycles, so caching each cell's answer makes it O(r · c).

Spot it: Edges go only from smaller to larger values, so the grid is an implicit DAG with no cycles. DFS from each cell, with memoization so each cell is computed once.

Approach:

  1. dfs(r, c) = length of the longest increasing path starting at (r, c).
  2. It's 1 + max(dfs(neighbour)) over the in-bounds neighbours with a larger value, or 1 if there are none.
  3. Cache the results in a dict self.memo keyed by (row, col). No visited set is needed, because "strictly increasing" rules out cycles.
  4. Return the maximum of dfs over all cells.
class Solution:
    def longestIncreasingPath(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        self.matrix = matrix
        self.rows = len(matrix)
        self.cols = len(matrix[0])
        self.memo = {}                 # (row, col) -> answer, so each cell is solved once
        best = 0
        for row in range(self.rows):
            for col in range(self.cols):
                length = self.dfs(row, col)
                if length > best:
                    best = length
        return best

    # Length of the longest increasing path that STARTS at (row, col).
    def dfs(self, row: int, col: int) -> int:
        if (row, col) in self.memo:    # solved before: reuse the answer
            return self.memo[(row, col)]
        best = 1                       # the cell by itself
        directions = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]  # down, up, right, left
        for direction in directions:
            next_row = row + direction[0]
            next_col = col + direction[1]
            inside = 0 <= next_row < self.rows and 0 <= next_col < self.cols
            if inside and self.matrix[next_row][next_col] > self.matrix[row][col]:
                candidate = 1 + self.dfs(next_row, next_col)  # strictly larger = no cycles
                if candidate > best:
                    best = candidate
        self.memo[(row, col)] = best   # remember it for next time
        return best

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. longestIncreasingPath saves the matrix, its size and an empty self.memo dict on self.
  2. It calls dfs(row, col) for every cell and keeps the largest result in best.
  3. In dfs, if (row, col) is already in the memo, we return the saved answer: each cell is solved only once.
  4. Otherwise best = 1 (the cell alone). For each of the 4 directions we compute the neighbour's row and column, check it is inside the grid and strictly larger, and if so try 1 + dfs(neighbour).
  5. We save the best length in the memo before returning it. No visited set is needed: values must strictly increase, so a path can't loop.

  • A single cell → 1.
  • A long snake-shaped increasing path.

Complexity: O(R·C) time and space.

Easy 112. Path Sum Binary Tree

Problem: Return True if some root-to-leaf path has values adding up to targetSum.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: root = [5,4,8,11,null,13,4,7,2,null,null,null,1], targetSum = 22
Output: true
Explanation: The root-to-leaf path with the target sum is shown.
Example 2
Input: root = [1,2,3], targetSum = 5
Output: false
Explanation: There are two root-to-leaf paths in the tree: (1 --> 2): The sum is 3. (1 --> 3): The sum is 4. There is no root-to-leaf path with sum = 5.

Constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000]. · -1000 ≤ Node.val ≤ 1000 · -1000 ≤ targetSum ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Carry the remaining sum down the tree.

Hint 2

At a leaf, check whether the remaining sum equals the leaf's value.

From brute force to the pattern: Collecting every root-to-leaf path and summing it is O(n · h). Passing the remainder down checks each path as you reach its leaf: O(n).

Spot it: Root-to-leaf paths → DFS that carries state downward. Subtracting each node's value from the target means a leaf only has to check whether what is left equals its own value.

Approach:

  1. An empty tree has no paths: False.
  2. Subtract the current node's value from the remaining sum.
  3. At a leaf (no children), succeed if the remainder is exactly 0.
  4. Otherwise succeed if either child's subtree has a path for the new remainder.
class Solution:
    def hasPathSum(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], targetSum: int) -> bool:
        if root is None:
            return False
        remaining = targetSum - root.val
        if root.left is None and root.right is None:
            # a leaf: the path ends here, so nothing may be left over
            return remaining == 0
        # keep going down either side with what is still needed
        return self.hasPathSum(root.left, remaining) or self.hasPathSum(root.right, remaining)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if root is None: return False: reached from a node with only one child. That is not a leaf, so no valid path ends here.
  2. remaining = targetSum - root.val: how much the rest of the path must still add up to.
  3. if root.left is None and root.right is None: the path must end at a leaf, so check the remainder only here.
  4. return ... or ...: try the left subtree, and only if that fails, the right one.

  • An empty tree → False, even if targetSum = 0.
  • A node with one child is not a leaf.
  • Negative values.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion space.

Medium 129. Sum Root to Leaf Numbers Google Meta Binary Tree

Problem: Each node holds a digit 0..9, and every root-to-leaf path spells a number (1 → 2 → 3 is 123). Return the sum of all these numbers.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: root = [1,2,3]
Output: 25
Explanation: The root-to-leaf path 1->2 represents the number 12. The root-to-leaf path 1->3 represents the number 13. Therefore, sum = 12 + 13 = 25.
Example 2
Input: root = [4,9,0,5,1]
Output: 1026
Explanation: The root-to-leaf path 4->9->5 represents the number 495. The root-to-leaf path 4->9->1 represents the number 491. The root-to-leaf path 4->0 represents the number 40. Therefore, sum = 495 + 491 + 40 = 1026.

Constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 1000]. · 0 ≤ Node.val ≤ 9 · The depth of the tree will not exceed 10.

Hint 1

Each root-to-leaf path spells a number.

Hint 2

Pass the number formed so far down the tree: number × 10 + node.val; add it to the total at each leaf.

From brute force to the pattern: Building each path as a string and converting it is O(n · h). Carrying the number down computes each path's value incrementally: O(n).

Spot it: Root-to-leaf + state that accumulates on the way down → DFS passing the partial number to the children.

Approach:

  1. dfs(node, number) receives the number formed by the path above node.
  2. Append this digit: number = number * 10 + node.val.
  3. At a leaf, the path's number is complete: return it.
  4. Otherwise return the sum of both children's results (a missing child contributes 0).
class Solution:
    def sumNumbers(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        def dfs(node, number):
            if node is None:
                return 0
            # shift the digits left and append this node's digit
            number = number * 10 + node.val
            if node.left is None and node.right is None:
                return number            # a complete root-to-leaf number
            return dfs(node.left, number) + dfs(node.right, number)

        return dfs(root, 0)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def dfs(node, number): number is passed by value, so each branch builds its own copy. No undoing is needed.
  2. if node is None: return 0: a missing child adds nothing.
  3. number = number * 10 + node.val: e.g. 12 followed by digit 3 → 123.
  4. if node.left is None and node.right is None: return number: a leaf finishes one number.
  5. return dfs(node.left, number) + dfs(node.right, number): add up every number below this node.

  • A single node.
  • Nodes with value 0 inside a path.
  • A node with one child.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) recursion space.

Medium 1448. Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree Google Binary Tree

Problem: A node is good if no node on the path from the root to it has a greater value. Count the good nodes.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: root = [3,1,4,3,null,1,5]
Output: 4
Explanation: Nodes in blue are good. Root Node (3) is always a good node. Node 4 -> (3,4) is the maximum value in the path starting from the root. Node 5 -> (3,4,5) is the maximum value in the path Node 3 -> (3,1,3) is the maximum value in the path.
Example 2
Input: root = [3,3,null,4,2]
Output: 3
Explanation: Node 2 -> (3, 3, 2) is not good, because "3" is higher than it.

Constraints: The number of nodes in the binary tree is in the range [1, 10^5]. · Each node's value is between [-10^4, 10^4].

Hint 1

A node is good if nothing on the path from the root to it is bigger.

Hint 2

DFS carrying the maximum value seen on the path so far.

From brute force to the pattern: For each node, walking back up to the root is O(n · h). Carrying the path maximum down decides each node in O(1): O(n).

Spot it: "Compared with everything on the path from the root" → DFS that carries the largest value seen so far.

Approach:

  1. dfs(node, max_so_far): max_so_far is the largest value on the path above node.
  2. If node.val >= max_so_far, this node is good: count 1.
  3. Update the maximum and add the counts from both children.
  4. Start with dfs(root, root.val): the root is always good.
class Solution:
    def goodNodes(self, root: TreeNode) -> int:
        def dfs(node, max_so_far):
            if node is None:
                return 0
            good = 0
            if node.val >= max_so_far:
                good = 1                      # nothing above it is bigger
            new_max = max(max_so_far, node.val)
            return good + dfs(node.left, new_max) + dfs(node.right, new_max)

        return dfs(root, root.val)

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. def dfs(node, max_so_far): each call knows the biggest value between the root and this node.
  2. if node.val >= max_so_far: good = 1: equal values still count as good ("no node greater").
  3. new_max = max(max_so_far, node.val): the path's maximum including this node, passed to both children.
  4. return good + dfs(...) + dfs(...): this node's contribution plus everything below it.

13no3
3 (under 1)3yes (3 ≥ 3)3
